idea: Aldus Manutius's dolphin-and-anchor printer's device, redrawn as a crisp engraving, with the Aldine motto 'FESTINA LENTE' and the small line 'Make haste slowly.' beneath it. For people who like a 500-year-old publisher's logo that still works as advice.

One column of the Gutenberg Bible in blackletter, with the lines counted down the margin in tiny numerals that stop at 42, then the caption '42 lines. Then everything.' A quiet nerd flex about the book that started printing with movable type in Europe.

The snail-versus-knight fight that turns up again and again in the margins of Gothic manuscripts, drawn as a pen-and-ink copy, with the caption 'The good stuff is in the margins.' For readers who annotate everything and like the monks' sense of humour.

An engraving of a compositor's two type cases stacked on their stand, the top one labelled 'UPPER CASE' and the bottom 'lower case', with the line 'Where the words came from.' The terms really do come from where printers kept capitals and small letters.

A woodcut-style monk slumped over his writing desk, with a real medieval scribe's colophon in Latin: 'Explicit hoc totum; pro Christo da mihi potum.' and the small translation 'That's the end of it. For Christ's sake, give me a drink.' For anyone who has ever finished a long piece of writing.

An ornate red-ink-style pilcrow drawn as a fine line, but with its own space left empty and a dotted outline, captioned 'The indent is where the ¶ used to be.' Scribes left gaps for rubricators to fill with pilcrows, and when nobody filled them the blank became the paragraph indent.

A row of letterforms going from a Roman cursive 'et' ligature to a Renaissance italic ampersand, captioned 'and, per se, and.' The schoolroom chant that gave the & its name, for type lovers who enjoy a character with a family tree.

A tight line drawing of the Rosetta Stone showing its three bands of hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek text, with the caption 'Same message. Three times. Just in case.' A wry nod to the over-communicator's stone that let Champollion crack hieroglyphs.

A plant illustration and lines of unknown script copied from the Voynich Manuscript, captioned 'Nobody can read it. Everybody has a theory.' For people who love a mystery that still hasn't been solved and are wary of anyone who claims to have solved it.

Samuel Johnson's 1755 dictionary entry typeset as it might appear on the page, with the long s and the original wording: 'LEXICO'GRAPHER. n.s. A writer of dictionaries; a harmless drudge.' A self-deprecating badge for editors, translators and anyone who sweats over words.

A small horned imp in a leather apron holding a composing stick, inked to the elbows, captioned 'PRINTER'S DEVIL' with the small definition 'n. the apprentice in a print shop.' A real trade term, for anyone who does the dirty work that keeps things running.

A single metal type sort drawn large in engraving style, the letter on its face shown mirrored, with the caption reversed on one line and readable below: 'Read it backwards to print it forwards.' A smart way of seeing how letterpress actually works.

The opening of William Caslon's 1734 specimen sheet, which begins with Cicero's 'Quousque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra?', with the small translation 'How long, Catiline, will you go on abusing our patience?' A classical way to say you're running out of patience, set in a classic English typeface.

A passage from Cicero's De finibus set in a Roman-style manuscript hand, with 'dolorem ipsum' circled and the 'do-' crossed out to leave 'lorem ipsum', captioned 'Cicero wrote it. Designers never read it.' Lorem ipsum really is scrambled Cicero, which makes this an inside joke for designers.

Jost Amman's 1568 woodcut 'Der Buchdrucker', showing pressmen inking type and pulling a sheet, captioned 'Every copy identical. That was the miracle.' A reminder that something we take for granted was once revolutionary.

An engraving of a stack of old folios, cut open to show a winding bookworm tunnel bored through every volume and a tiny larva at the end, captioned 'The original close reader.' Beetle larvae really did tunnel through old books, and this is for people who devour a book in one go.

A huge semicolon in an Aldine roman, with a small line underneath: 'Venice, 1496; the sentence isn't over.' Aldus Manutius was the first to print the semicolon, in Bembo's De Aetna, and this shirt is for people who won't give the semicolon up.

A careful drawing of the clay tablet in which a Babylonian named Nanni complains to the merchant Ea-nasir about bad copper, cuneiform and all, captioned 'Oldest surviving complaint letter. Still legible.' The written word has lasted almost four thousand years, and it has always been used to complain.

A Renaissance manicule (the little pointing hand readers drew in book margins), done as a fine engraving with a lace cuff, pointing at the words 'This part.' Earlier readers' version of a highlighter, for anyone who underlines.

A line in heavy blackletter from the 1631 'Wicked Bible', 'Thou shalt commit adultery.', with a small note: 'One missing word. The King's printers were fined £300.' A stern, funny case for proofreading.
